stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moreno's hypothesis?
stimulus: On rocky reefs off southern California, purple sea urchins can graze kelp forests down to bare rock. Marine ecologist Talia Moreno has observed that kelp tends to be denser on reefs patrolled by the California sheephead, a fish that preys on urchins. Moreno does not credit this pattern to sheephead eating large numbers of urchins. Instead, she hypothesizes that the fish's presence causes urchins to stay hidden in crevices, where they feed on drifting kelp fragments rather than grazing living kelp.
choices: Urchin densities were about the same on reefs with and without sheephead, but urchins on sheephead reefs spent much more of their time sheltered in crevices.
Reefs with sheephead had considerably more living kelp than reefs without sheephead did, and the difference was largest at the shallowest survey sites.
Urchins on both types of reef readily ate drifting kelp fragments whenever such fragments were available to them in crevices or on open rock.
Urchins were the most common prey item found in sheephead stomachs, and urchin densities were much lower on reefs where sheephead were present.
explanation: Moreno's hypothesis has two parts. The kelp difference is not caused by fewer urchins, and it is caused by urchins hiding. Choice A supports both. Urchin numbers match across the two reef types, which rules out predation as the cause, and urchins on sheephead reefs hide far more, which is the behavior Moreno proposes.

B.why: You picked a finding that restates the observation the hypothesis is trying to explain: there is more kelp where sheephead are. It says nothing about why, so it doesn't separate Moreno's explanation from the predation explanation she rejects.

C.why: You picked something that is true of both groups equally. If urchins everywhere eat drifting fragments, this finding can't explain why the two reef types differ. It only shows that urchins can eat fragments, not that sheephead make them hide.

D.why: This finding supports the explanation Moreno explicitly sets aside, that sheephead protect kelp by eating urchins and lowering their numbers. It works against her hypothesis.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the research team's conclusion?
stimulus: In a twelve-week trial, adults who took a daily inulin supplement showed smaller rises in blood glucose after meals than adults who took a placebo. Human enzymes cannot digest inulin. Instead, gut bacteria ferment it and release compounds such as butyrate. The research team concluded that inulin blunted the glucose rises not directly but through the butyrate that bacteria produced from it.
choices: Inulin participants' glucose rises after meals shrank steadily across the twelve weeks, while placebo participants' rises stayed about the same throughout.
Inulin participants given an antibiotic that suppressed gut bacteria produced little butyrate and had glucose rises similar to placebo participants' rises.
Blood butyrate levels increased by similar amounts in the inulin participants and the placebo participants over the course of the twelve-week trial.
Inulin participants reported feeling fuller after meals and, on average, ate smaller portions than placebo participants did at nearly every meal.
explanation: The conclusion is a chain: inulin leads to bacterial butyrate, and butyrate leads to smaller glucose rises. Inulin alone is not supposed to do it. Choice B removes the middle link while keeping the inulin. With bacteria suppressed, butyrate stays low and the benefit disappears. That shows the effect depends on butyrate, just as the team concluded.

A.why: You picked a finding that restates the observed result, that inulin users had smaller glucose rises. It never mentions butyrate, so it can't show that butyrate is the cause.

C.why: If butyrate rose equally in both groups, butyrate can't explain why only the inulin group improved. This finding is true of both groups equally and undercuts the proposed mechanism.

D.why: This points to a different cause, eating less, rather than the butyrate mechanism the team proposed. A competing explanation doesn't support their conclusion.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Arata's conclusion?
stimulus: Soft, water-saturated ground can intensify earthquake shaking, but it does not do so evenly. After a moderate earthquake struck near a coastal city, seismologist Kenji Arata compared recordings from instruments on artificially reclaimed harbor land with recordings from instruments on nearby bedrock. Arata concluded that the reclaimed land amplified slow, long-period ground motion but had little effect on rapid, short-period motion.
choices: Overall peak shaking at the reclaimed-land stations was greater than at the bedrock stations, and several harbor structures were damaged during the earthquake.
Reclaimed-land stations recorded about three times the bedrock stations' motion at both long periods and short periods throughout the earthquake.
Reclaimed-land stations recorded about three times the bedrock stations' long-period motion but roughly the same short-period motion as the bedrock stations.
Reclaimed-land stations recorded about the same long-period motion as the bedrock stations but roughly three times their short-period motion.
explanation: Arata's conclusion has two parts: amplification at long periods and little or no amplification at short periods. Choice C confirms both. It is the only choice that separates the two kinds of motion the way the conclusion does.

A.why: You picked a finding that confirms only that the reclaimed land shook more overall. It doesn't distinguish long-period motion from short-period motion, which is the whole point of the conclusion.

B.why: This supports a broader claim, that the reclaimed land amplifies all shaking. Arata said short-period motion was barely affected, so amplification at both periods goes against the limit set by the word 'but'.

D.why: This reverses the two parts. It puts the amplification at short periods and none at long periods, the opposite of what Arata concluded.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's conclusion?
stimulus: When wildfire burns intensely, waxy compounds vaporized from plant litter can condense on cooler soil grains below the surface and form a layer that repels water. Rain that would normally soak in then runs off the slope. After a fire swept unevenly through the Alder Creek basin, hydrologist Rosa Lindqvist concluded that the basin's sharply increased storm runoff came mainly from its severely burned slopes, not from its lightly burned ones.
choices: Storm runoff from the Alder Creek basin after the fire was roughly double the runoff produced by similar storms in the years before the fire.
Soil samples from severely and lightly burned slopes showed water-repellent layers of similar strength and absorbed similar amounts of simulated rain.
Severely burned slopes in several other basins that burned the same year also developed water-repellent layers within a few weeks of the fire.
Soil from severely burned slopes had a strong water-repellent layer and absorbed little simulated rain, while soil from lightly burned slopes absorbed rain normally.
explanation: Lindqvist's conclusion contrasts two groups of slopes: severely burned slopes produced the runoff and lightly burned slopes did not. Choice D separates them in exactly that way. It also links each group to the middle step of the passage's chain, the water-repellent layer that turns rain into runoff.

A.why: You picked a finding that restates the observed result, that runoff increased. It treats the basin as a whole, so it can't show which slopes the extra water came from.

B.why: This finding is true of both groups equally. If both kinds of slope repel water to the same degree, nothing explains why the severely burned slopes would produce most of the runoff. It undercuts the contrast in the conclusion.

C.why: You went beyond the basin Lindqvist studied. Findings from other basins say nothing about how severely and lightly burned slopes in Alder Creek compare.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nandakumar's claim?
stimulus: Concrete inevitably cracks, and water seeping into the cracks corrodes the steel reinforcement inside. Materials engineer Priya Nandakumar prepared two sets of concrete beams that were identical except that one set contained dormant bacterial spores and a calcium-based nutrient. When water enters a crack, the spores revive and deposit calcium carbonate. After cracking both sets and keeping them wet for six weeks, Nandakumar claimed that the bacteria enabled the concrete to seal narrow cracks but provided no benefit for wide ones.
choices: Narrow cracks in the bacterial beams sealed completely within the six weeks, and calcium carbonate deposits were found lining the sealed cracks.
Narrow cracks sealed in the bacterial beams but not in the ordinary beams, while wide cracks stayed open in both sets of beams.
Both narrow and wide cracks sealed in the bacterial beams, while neither narrow nor wide cracks sealed in the ordinary beams.
Narrow cracks sealed in both the bacterial beams and the ordinary beams, while wide cracks stayed open in both sets of beams.
explanation: The claim has two parts. For narrow cracks, the bacterial beams do better than the ordinary ones. For wide cracks, the two sets show no difference. Choice B confirms both parts and compares the matched groups, so the sealing can be credited to the bacteria, the only thing that differed.

A.why: You picked a finding that confirms only one part. It shows that narrow cracks sealed in the bacterial beams, but without the ordinary beams you can't tell whether the bacteria made a difference, and it says nothing about wide cracks.

C.why: This supports a stronger claim than Nandakumar made, that the bacteria help with all cracks. She said they provide no benefit for wide cracks, so this finding goes beyond her claim.

D.why: This finding is true of both groups equally. If ordinary beams sealed narrow cracks just as well, the bacteria made no difference, which contradicts the first part of the claim.
